Introduction

The development of new chemical processes and functional materials has traditionally followed a human-centered, Edisonian approach, based on manual experimentation using conventional laboratory glassware1,2,3,4. While this methodology has historically driven many a scientific breakthrough, it is unable to meet the ever-growing demand for high-performance materials1,5,6. The low experimental throughput of human-centered experimental sciences further slows scientific progress, while the large volumes typically used in benchtop experiments consume excessive material, further compounding the traditional approach’s inefficiency1,3. Additionally, the complexity of the high-dimensional parameter spaces intrinsic to chemical synthesis and materials processing precludes feasible exploration and optimization using either Edisonian approaches or human intuition1,4,7,8. Hence, the research community has begun to embrace autonomous robotic chemistry and materials research platforms commonly known as “self-driving laboratories” (SDLs).
Conceptual overview of SDLs

Fundamentally, SDLs integrate robotic automation with artificial intelligence (AI)–driven decision-making to enable time- and material-efficient closed-loop experimentation requiring no human intervention1,4,5,9. They are autonomous in the sense that they can make independent decisions and adapt their operation to changing experimental conditions with no human intervention. This represents a transformative approach that dramatically accelerates discoveries in chemistry and materials science by automating the design, execution, and analysis of experiments in a feedback-driven fashion, executing a design-make-test-analyze loop (Fig. 1)1,3,10. This Perspective article will focus on the usage of robots as individual, yet orchestrated components of the larger automated, and autonomous whole that is the SDL, as well as elucidating the common elements shared by most examples thereof1,2,11,12.
Types of robots in SDLs

Robots serve as the physical backbones of SDLs, enabling reliable execution of experimental workflows and ensuring seamless handoff between synthesis, processing, and analytical steps6,9,13,14,15,16. SDLs can integrate a wide array of robotic subsystems, fulfilling a multitude of different roles (Fig. 2). These subsystems can be broadly classified by their structural characteristics (e.g., robotic arms), or operational functions (e.g., liquid or solid handling, characterization)6,16. They may be commercial turnkey platforms, or they might be bespoke, custom-made robots, perhaps incorporating additive manufacturing (AM) methods in their construction and employ open-source software16,17,18.
Robotic arms

Since modern robotic arms first emerged in the 1960s in automotive industry, two primary architectures have come to dominate both industrial and scientific automation: six-axis articulated arms (also known as six-degrees of freedom [DOF]), and SCARAs (Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arms)19,20,21,22,23,24,25,26.

SCARAs consist of a central column with two rotational joints that enable movement in the XY plane. The arm assembly is capable of vertical actuation along the Z-axis, with the end effector affixed thereto via a compliant joint, capable of flexion. This allows for rapid, high-precision movements, making them ideal for tasks requiring speed and repeatability not involving complex spatial object manipulation20,21,23. In contrast, six-DOF arms provide mostly unconstrained positioning, mimicking the flexibility of a human arm at the expense of speed and kinematic simplicity20,26,27. Nevertheless, they offer unmatched versatility, being capable of much more sophisticated maneuvers than SCARAs. In contemporary SDLs, such flexibility often serves to bind the SDL’s instruments together into a functional whole. Six-DOF robotic arms can typically execute most of the manipulation tasks required in an SDL: including vial transfers, reagent addition, and usage of otherwise manual instruments28,29,30.
Liquid handling robots

Automated liquid-handling platforms are another cornerstone of many SDLs, being particularly well-suited to solution-phase chemistries15,31. They enable high-precision liquid handling, eliminating variability introduced by manual pipetting as well as dramatically increasing throughput32. The majority of commercial liquid handling robots rely on either air-displacement pipette-based or fixed-probe-based architectures to perform liquid handling15,33. Air displacement pipettes are commonly used for aqueous media, whereas positive displacement pipettes are preferred for viscous or volatile solvent32. Liquid handling robots offer scalable configurations supporting parallel processing and combinatorial experimentation15,18,31,34. These systems frequently serve as the primary reagent handling and mixing units of SDLS, often operating together with robotic arms and analytical instrumentation under centralized software frameworks14,34.

Pipette or probe-based liquid handlers exhibit optimal accuracy when dispensing in the range of tens to hundreds of microliters32. Smaller volumes, e.g., in the nanoliter regime, require alternative techniques. Acoustic liquid handling, for example, can precisely deposit nanoliter droplets onto vessels such as 384-well plates and has become increasingly relevant for ultra-low volume workflows35. Furthermore, liquid handlers are often equipped with on-deck modules that extend their functionality, including temperature control systems, washing stations, centrifuges, and even microscale chemical reactors operating under pressurized or elevated-temperature conditions15. Some even incorporate robotic arms or grippers to facilitate the transfer of labware or reagents between modules or deck positions15.

The utility of liquid handling robots is particularly pronounced in high-throughput applications, such as combinatorial chemistry, AI-driven optimization, and large-scale screening campaigns1,15. Liquid handling robots can serve as a flexible and reliable foundation for the construction of modular SDL platforms suited to an extremely wide array of chemical and materials science tasks.
Characterization instruments

Characterization instruments are a sine qua non for SDLs: an SDL would not be complete without some means of collecting data from its experiments. However, characterization instruments are amongst the least integration-friendly components of an SDL16. Analytical instruments such as gas or liquid chromatography units, microplate readers, mass spectrometers, microscopes, and spectroscopy instruments–while often automated in that they can execute user-designed workflows via a desktop software suite–are seldom-designed with the possibility of the instrument’s integration into a larger autonomous system as a consideration: on a software level or a hardware level16. However, some SDL-friendly instruments exist, often allowing for their operation to be programmatically controlled by custom user-written code courtesy of vendor-provided application programming interfaces (APIs). In essence, an API is a collection of code functions or software objects that can be incorporated into the user’s program to, in the case of laboratory automation, communicate with an instrument, monitor its status, issue commands to it and retrieve data. Many researchers have resorted to using robots to operate manual instruments, or creatively modifying existing instruments for incorporation into an SDL5. It has even proven necessary to design and build characterization instruments from scratch5,16. Such a state of affairs is unlikely to last indefinitely: as SDLs become ever more prominent, vendors will likely adapt by designing products with SDLs in mind, filling this commercial void16.
Bespoke vs. commercial robots

Commercial, off-the-shelf (COTS) robotic systems provide standardized, modular solutions for automating repetitive and time-sensitive tasks in chemistry and materials science laboratory environments. Their widespread availability allows for the development time of an SDL to be dramatically shortened, especially for workflows with well-defined, common operations. While COTS robotic systems often involve substantial capital investment, they offer established reliability, vendor support, and software compatibility that can be essential for maintaining operational robustness16. Off-the-shelf solutions may often lack the requisite customizability for highly specialized tasks, yet they nevertheless play a vital role in the SDL ecosystem12,16.

Liquid handling robots constitute an example of this dichotomy: while COTS liquid handling robots offer robust performance, their cost–averaging ~$40k USD per unit–can limit accessibility33. In response, the scientific community has pursued the development of low-cost, open-source alternatives. These often leverage additive manufacturing, laser cutting, and cost-effective open-source microcontrollers, to create modular liquid handling systems from inexpensive components. The FINDUS platform, for instance, retrofits an off-the-shelf manual pipette into an automated system together with a custom-designed and largely additively-manufactured peptide synthesis module17. Other cost-effective examples include the Sidekick platform, which utilizes integrated pumps and tubing to dispense liquids into 96-well plates at a total cost of ~$710 USD, and the EvoBot platform, which combines gantry motion with syringe-driven liquid handling36,37.

The principal disadvantages of do-it-yourself (DIY) robots, however, are their lengthy development times, the need for potentially substantial expertise in software engineering or electronics, or potentially inadequate performance or reliability16. Nevertheless, DIY robots play a key role in lowering economic barriers to entry for SDLs and filling the void left by vendors concerning relatively uncommon or completely novel experimental tasks.
Examples of robotics usage in SDLs

The integration of orchestrated robots in SDLs has enabled boosted experimental throughput with reliable and reproducible synthesis and characterization. Leveraging AI-assisted decision-making, SDLs have the capability to accelerate discovery, development, and optimization of functional materials and molecules (Table 1).
Ada

One real-world example of robotics usage in SDLs may be found in Ada (Fig. 3A), a modular SDL designed by MacLeod et al. for the autonomous optimization of optoelectronic properties of thin-film materials38. At Ada’s core lay a multi-purpose polar robotic arm, capable of reaching every workstation therein, which also had a rotatable pneumatic gripper attached to its end that it used to interact with vials with high accuracy, boasting a repeatability of 10 µm38. It also incorporated a syringe pump-powered pipette head mounted to the arm’s end that was tasked with liquid transfers, achieving a mean accuracy of 5 µL.

Ada’s workflow entailed aspirating precursor solutions from their stock containers and mixing them together in a vial on atop a scale, followed by drop-casting the mixture onto a substrate using a spin coater, said substrate thereafter being moved to an annealing oven using a vacuum-sealing functional slide handler, where an automated heat gun annealed the slide for an amount of time recommended by Ada’s AI agent, after which the robotic arm carried the sample to multiple instruments for multi-modal characterization, including imaging, and measuring optical spectra and conductance. The results were then provided to the Phoenics Bayesian optimization (BO) algorithm to generate the next set of experimental conditions to maximize the resulting material’s hole mobility. Owing to its combination of Phoenics BO with a robotic platform, Ada demonstrated the ability of SDLs to explore the dizzyingly complex parameter space of thin film organic hole transport materials far more rapidly effectively than with conventional high-throughput experimentation techniques. Ada’s experiments also revealed an unexpected dynamic wherein heavily-doped thin-films, past a certain point, become more thermally stable than their less-doped counterparts.

Ada managed to identify the precursor dosage ratio and annealing time that yielded the maximum of hole mobility within 30 samples, with the sequential synthesis-characterization-planning of each sample taking less than 21 min to finish. Ada’s efficiency substantially benefitted from its multipurpose polar robotic arm, together with its quick tool changing and integration of multiple end effectors, which eliminated the need for deploying other dedicated robots.
Rainbow

In contrast to Ada’s single-robot approach, Rainbow is a multi-robotic SDL for synthesis science studies and optimization of metal halide perovskite nanocrystals via bespoke orchestration of 4 robots tasked with performing material synthesis, characterization, waste management, and labware replenishment (Fig. 3B)34. A pipette-based liquid handling robot was charged with all liquid handling tasks involved in material synthesis, such as mixing multiple precursors, material sampling, and unwanted material collection. Additionally, a stationary, mechanical gripper-equipped six-DOF robot capable of reaching all crucial spots inside of the platform successfully carried out pick-and-place tasks via pre-defined trajectories. A robotic benchtop spectrometer also automatically captured samples’ UV-Vis absorption and photoluminescence spectra. After an experimental iteration, the robotic arm disposed of contaminated consumables such as well plates and pipette tips, replacing them with fresh consumables of the same type that were housed in a custom-built and additively-manufactured robotic instrument, the “plate feeder”. This robot ensured that fresh labware was always available at the same position in space, allowing the robotic arm to consistently and accurately restock the liquid handler without being thwarted by positional inaccuracies. Through the reliability, reproducibility, and throughput afforded it by its robotic components, Rainbow identified the best ligand structures and precursor concentrations for metal halide perovskite nanocrystals within one day–a 350x acceleration vs. human-centered exploration—and provided further insights into the complicated relationship between ligand choices and these nanocrystals’ structures, syntheses, and properties.
Mobile chemist

While Ada and Rainbow demonstrated the power of orchestrated robots in fast-tracked experimentation, they required careful design to ensure that all of their different components were within reach of their stationary robotic arms. However, multi-step operations and multimodal characterization are necessary for more complicated chemistry and material synthesis, so the incorporation of more robots or workstations in SDLs becomes a necessity3,39. Even so, the overall reach of a stationary robotic arm limits an SDL’s size and complexity and caps the number of extra components that can be incorporated whilst still being within the robotic arm’s reach. In order to bypass this problem, mobile robots are becoming increasingly favored to navigate complex SDL layouts9,14,40.

An early, seminal example of mobile robots being used in SDLs, (as well as an early example of robotic SDLs in general), may be found in the “mobile robotic chemist” of Burger et al., which is an SDL dedicated to accelerated photocatalyst development9, shown in Fig. 3C. This SDL’s robotic arm, equipped with a multipurpose gripper, was mounted atop a mobile robot. This configuration eliminated most of the robotic arm length and reach limitations affecting Rainbow and Ada. Instead, after the fashion of a human chemist, this robot was deployed in a conventional chemistry lab with all necessary implements and workstations. It could perform most of the dexterous manipulations necessary for carrying out its experiments without hardware modifications, although purpose-built capping and photolysis stations were still necessary. Its customized gripper could grasp different objects, including 10 mL gas chromatography (GC) vials and solid dispensing cartridges9. The mobile chemist finished a batch of 16 experiments within 481 min and continuously ran over eight days for 688 experiments, reaching a 1000-fold and >10-fold research acceleration compared to manual experiments and semi-automated robotic workflow, respectively. Through accurate navigation, paired with human-like size, reach, and dexterity, the multi-purpose gripper, this robot was able to access more than 15 times more space than ADA and Rainbow, functioning on par with human chemists in a space designed for humans, implying such SDLs are eminently compatible with existing research infrastructure9,34,38.
A-lab

While most SDLs are constrained to liquid phase reactions given the ease of dispensing and mixing liquids, solid-phase reactions are often needed in materials science research and development14. SDLs such as A-lab have been emerging to bridge this gap29. A-Lab was an automated platform built to bridge computational screening and experimental testing of novel inorganic materials in powder form, shown in Fig. 3D. It consisted of three integrated stations designed for sample preparation, carrying out reactions, and characterization, with three robotic arms transferring samples within or between stations. An automatic dispenser balance dispensed prescribed amounts of precursor powders into plastic vials, which were then mixed thoroughly with ethanol and ZrO2 balls in a centrifuge to form a viscous slurry that was then automatically pipetted into an alumina crucible and dried at 80 °C in a closed evaporation system29. Next, a linear rail-mounted robotic arm, (allowing the circumvention of said arm’s reach limitations), transferred the crucible containing the samples into one of four box furnaces whose doors were controlled by custom actuators. The samples were heated, and then cooled down inside the furnaces, the robotic arm retrieved them to allow for further cooling to room temperature. The stationary robotic arm at this station poured the powders into a vial covered by a steel mesh, inverting it to dispense them onto an X-ray diffraction (XRD) sample holder, followed by a flattening step with an acrylic disc. The robotic arm then carried the sample to the diffractometer for XRD analysis. A-Lab performed 355 back-to-back experiments in 17 days, verifying 41 of the 58 novel inorganic crystalline solids predicted by density functional theory (DFT) computational screening and active-learning feedback, thereby demonstrating that SDLs can also be applied to solid-phase reactions and generate new scientific insights thereby.
Challenges, limitations, and opportunities
Hardware selection and integration

A typical first step in building an SDL is the selection of devices, instruments, and robots necessary to carry out the workflow, with the accurate identification of necessary tolerances, layouts, ancillary hardware and components, operating requirements, and design constraints imposed by such factors as budgets, available space, and the realities of the facility that will house that SDL being a vital corollary16. Oversights, changing requirements, or unexpected hiccups can lead to substantial problems in the construction of an SDL, be it lengthened development time or extra equipment costs. These developments are often unpredictable, with some issues, deficiencies, and incompatibilities only being discoverable after the robots and hardware have been acquired, and they can have significant ripple effects—often contributing substantially to the lengthy development times seen in constructing SDLs8.

This problem can be especially prominent when integrating and using robots and instruments from multiple vendors and can be further compounded by vendor design decisions that reduce or hinder compatibility, sometimes requiring substantial measures to remedy (e.g., the acquisition or construction of additional robots or instruments)5,12,16. Early in the development of the Rainbow SDL mentioned earlier, we intended to simply place stacks of labware on the floor of the enclosure in designated spots, which would then be used by Rainbow’s central robotic arm to replenish consumed labware, however, the problems associated with this approach necessitated additional robots.
Orchestrating robots in SDLs

In addition to the hardware-based travails often encountered when constructing and operating an SDL, software also presents its own set of challenges. In order to control an instrument or robot via a central program written with the intention of governing and orchestrating an SDL’s overall workflow, an instrument-specific API is often needed16,41,42. Vendors often do not provide these APIs to build an SDL16,43,44. Additionally, these APIs are far from standardized: they can be found using a dizzying array of implementation frameworks and can take a tremendous number of different forms: ranging from a set of rudimentary firmware commands to be issued to the device by the user’s program, or they can be more complex interfaces associated with the instrument’s own software that allow other programs to communicate with the instrument16,43,44.

Software for orchestrating the different components of an SDL tends to be just as unstandardized, if not more so16. Oftentimes, the orchestration software for a given SDL is brittle, i.e., prone to failure when modified, by virtue of being purpose-built and tightly-coupled to its specific platform2. Such software is rarely capable of generalizing to other platforms meant to carry out a different research task, or platforms with different hardware composition. In response, a number of nascent device-agnostic orchestration frameworks aimed at solving these twin problems have come into being, such as ChemOS, χDL, and PyLabRobot amongst others41,42,44,45. In addition, more mature examples of software capable of controlling robots, such as LabView and ROS, have also been used for SDL orchestration46,47,48. Some examples may revolve around a particular type of robot, such as PyLabRobot and its current narrow focus on liquid handlers. Others, such as ROS, aim to be far more general frameworks for robot orchestration beyond, yet incidentally and theoretically including SDLs. Others still, such as χDL are aimed specifically at SDLs, with an emphasis on the protocol code constructed therewith being portable, i.e., capable of running identically on different SDL platforms with no modifications, the results thereof similarly comporting. However, as Canty et al. note in their 2024 article, this last objective has proven elusive for frameworks such as χDL that rely on more abstract representations of the individual operations comprising the workflow–abstract in the sense that these representations decouple the specification of the task itself from the machine-specific details and logistics necessary to carry it out43.

This reproducibility dilemma stems at least in part from the sometimes-radical differences in design between different examples of a robot type, which the orchestration software framework necessarily ignores, and treats any two components in the same role identically43. Canty et al. give the example of liquid handling tasks such as dispensing, and note that the differences in precision, accuracy, and operating principle between two different models of liquid handling robots constitute a non-triviality that cannot be ignored if a researcher wishes, (as they ought), to ensure that their experiments are reproducible43,49,50,51.
SDL safety and fault tolerance

SDLs, by virtue of their autonomous operation, are beneficial where the safety of their operators is concerned: they can handle dangerous chemicals that would otherwise pose a substantial, or even unacceptable risk to the operator; nevertheless, SDLs also pose potential safety risks of their own5,52,53. Some salient examples noted in the literature include collisions between robots, or robots and operators; the unintentional generation of extremely hazardous chemical compounds, toxic, explosive, or otherwise; failures of key robotic components of the SDL; as well as attacks by malicious actors or dual-use scenarios52. While many of these hazards can be mitigated during the design stage, unexpected hazards can emerge during normal operation as well52,53,54. As SDLs continue to grow more complex and generalizable, however, it will become necessary for the SDLs themselves to be capable of recognizing, predicting, and avoiding unsafe conditions—the solutions to some of these challenges could potentially be found in new developments in the field of robotics: such as Ni et al’s newly-developed approach of “SAFETY-AS-POLICY” that uses world models to train LMM-based (large multimodal models) cognitive models to allow intelligent robots to recognize, or even predict and mitigate hazards in situ54.
The future of robotics in SDLs

Across the fields of robotics and machine learning at large, as well as the field of SDLs in particular, a sizable assortment of potentially transformative technologies and paradigms are beginning to emerge where it concerns software, hardware, applications, design, and undergirding principles and theories. Some of these developments may have profound implications for SDLs and could open up new possibilities in their usage, construction, and operation, and aid their broader adoption. Here we present some areas which we believe can shape the future of robotics in SDLs.
Swarm robotics

Swarm robotics as a field concerns the control and orchestration of multiple robots without any centralized control, instead using a set of simple rules from which the necessary behavior to carry out the system’s intended function simply emerges as a consequence of the interactions between its simple robotic components55. Owing to their decentralized nature and the relative simplicity of each individual robot comprising the swarm, and the resilience of swarms in the face of unexpected conditions, swarm robotics represents a potentially highly useful design paradigm for SDL robotics that could allow them to emulate the flexibility and functionality of human labs in full, an imagined example being shown in (Fig. 4A). The usage of true swarm robotics in SDLs is, to the best of our knowledge, nonexistent in published work. There have, however, been demonstrations of SDLs using a collection of small, independent mobile robots for sample transfer that are tantalizingly adjacent to true robotic swarms, a salient example being Mariano et. al’s recent work wherein a centrally-controlled fleet of small, cheap mobile robots with some limited autonomy ferried samples between several different robotic workstations in the SwissCat+ laboratory56,57.

If the swarm robotics paradigm is to be applied to SDLs, however, then it necessitates moving past conventional, homogeneous swarms of simple robots to heterogeneous swarms of many kinds of robots, varying in complexity, shape, and purpose. Much progress has already been made to that end, with a notable early example being Dorigo et al.’s 2013 paper on what they referred to as “Swarmanoid”, a demonstration of a heterogeneous swarm containing three distinct types of robot collaborating on a single task58. Should this paradigm be successfully applied to SDLs, it would obviate the need for centralized orchestration, owing to its intrinsically decentralized nature. An additional capability and prerequisite for implementing an SDL from the ground up as a heterogeneous swarm is the ability to multitask59. Hence, heterogeneity and multitasking are both necessary for a swarm-based SDL that can, sans human intervention or a centralized orchestrating software component, conduct multiple experiments, autonomous troubleshooting and maintenance; self-reconfiguration as needed for a different workflow; and management of its own logistics. Additionally, given that swarm robots can be small and simple, they may be eminently-suited to deployment in confined lab spaces, which Swiss Cat+ as described by Mariano et al partially demonstrates56,60.
Autonomous maintenance and reconfiguration for new tasks

A notable current limitation of SDLs that precludes truly complete autonomy is the need for human intervention between experimental campaigns in the form of maintenance. To the best of our knowledge, this appears to be the case in nearly every example of an SDL published in the literature to date. Moreover, the failure of a robotic instrument and its repair also requires extensive human intervention. There are ongoing attempts to create actionable frameworks for implementing self-maintenance in SDLs, with one notable example being Ochiai et al.’s 2025 article: therein, they introduce the SDL-specific concept of self-maintainability (SeM), wherein a thusly-capable SDL can autonomously handle all of the necessary logistical tasks to remain operational–albeit sans autonomous installation and de-installation of robotic hardware or instruments (Fig. 4B)61.

Ochiai et al.’s proposed abstract scheme for implementing SeM in SDLs includes three principal components tasked with managing labware, devices, and requirements, all in turn managed by a central module that integrates them with an AI model and a scheduler61. The management of requirements entails an interactive process where the system gathers initial information in the form of natural language, (either spoken or written), from the user concerning the latter’s desired experiment, and acquires additional information from the user as deemed necessary while the system carries out the necessary planning, maintenance, and reconfiguration tasks to carry out the desired experiments. Device management takes the form of generation of experimental code and protocols to control and orchestrate the SDL’s hardware components to implement the workflow. Lastly, labware management entails sensor-based tracking and detection of the SDL’s condition to ensure that nothing disrupts the workflow from running and managing or remedying such impediments as they emerge.

Until and unless SDLs can incorporate fully-autonomous maintenance, the vision of truly closed-loop SDL autonomy will never be realized. Robot designs must evolve into forms that lend themselves not only to autonomous installation and removal, but also to easy servicing by other robots. This will also require an expansion of the tooling available to robots in SDLs, such as the development of collections of robotic arm end effectors and tools that could be used for servicing, together with industry-standardized configurations of robots’ components, and perhaps new standards for lab space construction and usage62.
Adaptive morphogenesis, autonomous replication, and additive manufacturing

SDLs’ long-term viability depends upon their being reconfigurable for the execution of different workflows. Moreover, preservation of the definitional SDL design ethos of autonomy requires reconfiguration to be carried out sans human intervention—in other words, every step of the reconfiguration process ought to be carried out autonomously, from the fabrication of any necessary parts and modules, down to their installation and testing. A possible solution to this dilemma may be found by combining autonomous robotic implementations of adaptive morphogenesis, (a biology concept), and generative design with additive manufacturing63,64,65,66.

As Baines et al. point out in their 2024 review article, adaptive morphogenesis has essentially become a byword for “evolution on demand”64. Hence, the implementation of this concept in robotics entails furnishing robots with the ability to automatically adapt their construction and programming to new tasks or changed environments (Fig. 4C)63,64. This may take the form of design elements that allow for a robot to substantially alter its structure, and hence function, or perhaps a modular robot that is capable of self-alteration via the automatic installation and removal of modules.

An example might be a robotic welder based on a six-axis arm that can seamlessly swap between different types of welding torches, or even reconfigure itself to use drastically different welding methods depending on the properties of the workpiece. Paired with additive manufacturing, adaptive morphogenesis as implemented in SDL robotics may even entail de novo, in-situ generative design, fabrication, and installation of welding toolheads that are optimal for, say, welding thin aluminum filaments into a wireframe structure, whereas the currently-equipped toolhead might be best suited for welding large sections of cast iron together. In an SDL, this paradigm would take on a much broader scope, with SDLs’ adaptive morphogenetic capabilities ranging from minor tweaks to a particular robot’s operating specifications to the outright design and fabrication of new robotic modules as needed to execute newly-prescribed experiments. It is conceivable that such capabilities deployed in an SDL could require additional investment in facilities, owing to the need to accommodate additional fabrication equipment and may prove challenging to implement in a confined, shared lab space—though perhaps recent innovations in task and motion planning, as well as autonomous hazard prediction and mitigation could be of some help in allowing such a robotic system to safely coexist with human researchers in the same spaces54,67.
Conclusions

As advances occur in self-maintaining robotics, generative design, and autonomous small-scale, in-situ manufacturing, both the financial and temporal costs of SDLs will shrink apace, and render SDLs ever more accessible, diverse in function, and numerous. Similarly important in reducing developmental costs and difficulty of implementation, as well as increasing the robustness of SDLs are changes and standardizations in the fundamental methods of constructing robots, as well as their orchestration, with a greater emphasis on modularity, interoperability, and compatibility. Likewise, more sophisticated and flexible AI agents are also necessary to encompass the wide, and conceptually diverse range of tasks needed to not only design experimental workflows, but also to design and fabricate the necessary hardware and software components, as well as autonomously manage every aspect of the logistics of running an SDL. SDL researchers must, therefore, strive to stay abreast of advancements in robotics, AI, and the methods of integrating them.

Nevertheless, contemporary robotics-driven SDLs, limited as they may be in some respects, have already demonstrated an inherent ability to dramatically accelerate the pace and efficiency of research across multiple disciplines of the physical and life sciences, conducting experimental tasks running the gamut from chemical synthesis to device fabrication. However, in order for SDLs to become truly autonomous in the strictest sense of the word, and hence unlock their full potential, further advances in robotics and the development of ever-more capable AI agents are of the utmost necessity. Robots serve as the physical lynchpins for most types of non-fluidic SDLs, and just as the developments in robotics and automation have powered tremendous changes and advances in industry and society, so too could their use in SDLs have a profoundly transformative impact on how research is conducted across multiple fields, leading to a more distributed and democratized paradigm in which networks of SDLs conduct experiments at the request of scientists, institutions, and even ordinary citizens who may be geographically far-removed from the experiments autonomously conducted at their behest11.

2026-05-17T07:00:00Z,Who Controls the West: Nevada's New Data Center Boom – Sierra Nevada Ally,"Who Controls the West: Nevada’s New Data Center Boom

Across Northern Nevada, a massive buildout of data centers, AI infrastructure, and energy systems is transforming the desert into a backbone of the digital economy—reviving old questions about land, water, power, and who gets to decide how they are used.

This story is part of an ongoing series, Who Controls the West, which examines the people, companies and organizations that make decisions over how land and resources are used across the American West. Have ideas for the series? Email [email protected].

A business park known as the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center (TRIC) stretches across a landmass larger than the city of Denver. It is home to one of the largest data center campuses in the United States, built by the company Switch, alongside sprawling facilities owned by Google and Microsoft. Apple operates a separate complex nearby. Tesla’s Gigafactory is part of the same industrial corridor.
From above, it resembles a new kind of city. From the ground, it is something more fragmented: warehouses of computation scattered across the high desert.

In the mid-1800s, this same stretch of Nevada was an Old West boomtown. Storey County—which has since emerged as a major data center hub anchored by the TRIC—contained some of the richest deposits of gold and silver in the American West, earning it the nickname “the richest place on Earth.” Mark Twain came here as a miner and began his writing career reporting for a local newspaper, later describing the era in Roughing It as one where “money was as plenty as dust.”

In the American West, land and water have long been governed by systems that determine who can extract value from them, and on what terms. With the gold rush now long over, today’s Nevada sits at the center of a new boom driven by data center development.
AI infrastructure is now entering those same systems, not as a break from the region’s history, but as its newest chapter.
Why the Servers Come to the Desert
While artificial intelligence may appear intangible, the systems powering it are deeply physical.

Behind chatbots, image generators and cloud computing is a quieter physical world: sprawling warehouses of servers that store information and perform the immense calculations needed to train and run artificial intelligence systems. As demand for AI accelerates, companies like Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta are racing to expand data center infrastructure across the United States. Increasingly, that expansion is settling into the rural West.
Northern Nevada is emerging as one of the country’s fastest-growing data center corridors, with more than 40 facilities operating or planned across the Reno-Sparks region.

But the region’s emergence as an infrastructure hub is not accidental. The same conditions that once drew mining companies, railroads, and industrial manufacturers westward—open land, abundant resources and development-friendly policy—are now attracting the physical backbone of the digital economy.

Data centers require space, power, and long-term infrastructure commitments, all of which help explain Reno’s appeal. The region offers large stretches of industrial-zoned land, lower operating costs than California, and a strategic position between Silicon Valley and other Western markets. Nevada policymakers have also aggressively courted development through tax incentives. At RNO2, the data center currently under construction on Keystone Avenue, qualifying equipment and machinery could be eligible for a reduced 2% sales tax rate and a 75% abatement on personal property taxes.

TRIC was early in taking advantage of this and lay the groundwork for what was to come. In the late 1990s, developer Lance Gilman began assembling more than 100,000 acres of former Gulf Oil land and turned it into a privately-managed industrial zone with pre-approved land uses and fast-tracked permitting. That setup made large-scale development much easier and helped attract Tesla’s first Gigafactory in 2014, which transformed the area into a major hub for advanced manufacturing and logistics. Data centers soon followed.
Projects like CENTRA Reno’s RNO2 campus are designed to deepen Northern Nevada’s role in the regional flow of internet traffic, helping information move more quickly across the West.
But the same conditions fueling that growth also sharpen existing pressures.

“Beyond the resource challenges presented by data center growth, their expansion may offer opportunities to the state,” said Sean McKenna, executive director of the Division of Hydrologic Sciences at the Desert Research Institute. “Nevada has the potential to be a central player in the increasingly digital world, but there are challenges that must be resolved to ensure other stakeholders and priorities are balanced with the increasing demands of rapid data center expansion.”

Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity, rely on extensive cooling systems, and often require years of supporting infrastructure expansion in a region already grappling with mounting pressure over water, housing and energy demand.

As artificial intelligence continues to expand, the central question facing places like Northern Nevada is beginning to shift. The issue is no longer simply Why here?’ and more ‘How much can the region absorb before policy and infrastructure struggle to keep pace?’
Data Boomtown Economics

Constructing data centers is enormously expensive. Industry estimates place development costs at roughly $10 to $12 million per megawatt, even for relatively conventional facilities. At that scale, a single project can surpass $100 million long before a server ever comes online. Like many large-scale tech facilities, data centers are often promoted as engines of economic growth—bringing jobs, tax revenue and new investment to the region. In practice, the benefits tend to be more limited and uneven than those promises suggest.

But recent reporting showing large data center projects often create far fewer permanent jobs than public rhetoric suggests. RNO2 is expected to employ a relatively small on-site workforce. One local analysis estimated the facility would support around 11 on-site jobs with wages averaging roughly $31 per hour.

This gap between expectations and reality is not unique to Nevada. As The Nevada Independent has noted, data centers tend to function as low-employment but relatively stable tax-base industries—projects that can support public revenue over time, but only if they are carefully structured and governed. Otherwise, the economic upside can look very different on the ground than it does in policy discussions.
What About Water?
Alongside artificial intelligence, the other word that continually surfaces in conversations about data centers is water.

Water use has become one of the most contested aspects of data center expansion, particularly in arid regions like Nevada. Roughly two-thirds of data centers built or planned since 2022 are located in areas already experiencing high levels of water stress. In Nevada, one of the fastest-warming states in the country, decades of drought, rising temperatures, and declining snowpack have only intensified concerns over how much growth the region’s water systems can realistically sustain.

According to the Desert Research Institute, combining projected water-use efficiency and data center growth, total water demand could reach roughly 9,650 acre-feet per year, more than the annual amount needed for 27,600 U.S. households. On paper, that may sound abstract. In practice, it represents a new category of water demand layered onto an already constrained system—one that already divides supply among cities, agriculture, industry and tribal nations under a tightly regulated and historically contested water rights framework.

In Storey County, where average rainfall is just about 11 inches a year, that added demand has raised concerns among some residents and tribal communities. The Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, whose homeland lies downstream from the industrial corridor, has long depended on flows from the Truckee River—the same system that supplies water to parts of the industrial center. Any additional pressure on that system raises questions about cumulative impacts in a region where every drop is already allocated.
Because water has long been central to conflict over land, sovereignty, and survival in the West, concern over its proper use is now at the forefront of much of the opposition.

Indigenous-led groups and environmental coalitions, including the Water over Data Alliance, have pushed back against new development proposals, arguing that large-scale infrastructure is being added to a basin that is already under strain. Some proposals have even gone further, including ideas like installing AI-powered monitoring systems on rivers—efforts framed by supporters as conservation tools, but viewed by critics as a form of surveillance layered onto environmental management.

In response, developers are pointing to new technologies designed to reduce water demand. Some facilities use closed-loop cooling systems that can significantly limit ongoing water use. However, the tradeoff is that these systems often shift demand from water to electricity. Cooling is one the largest energy demands in a data center, accounting for roughly 30-40% of total electricity use.

In systems designed to reduce water consumption, that demand can shift toward electricity as mechanical cooling and heat rejection systems carry more of the load. Which is why, beneath the debate over water, the more immediate constraint is power.
Power Challenges

Nevada’s data centers already account for roughly 22% of the state’s electricity demand, with projections suggesting that share could grow substantially by 2030. NV Energy estimates that just a handful of planned projects—around 12 facilities statewide—could require about 5,900 megawatts of power, roughly 2.8 times the capacity of Hoover Dam. At 12 megawatts, the RNO2 facility would draw enough electricity to power roughly 120,000 desktop computers continuously.

As demand increases, utilities are increasingly faced with a balancing act: accommodating large new industrial users while maintaining reliability for residential customers. If grid expansion does not keep pace, strain on the system during peak periods, especially during extreme summer heat, can increase pressure on grid reliability. That risk is especially significant in Nevada, where temperatures regularly exceed 100 degrees and warming trends are intensifying across the region.

Those tensions are already beginning to surface elsewhere in the region. In the Lake Tahoe basin, NV Energy recently informed Liberty Utilities, which serves roughly 49,000 customers around Lake Tahoe, that it would stop supplying most of the utility’s power after 2027, citing growing internal demand. The decision has drawn national attention because it comes as electricity demand tied to data center expansion surges across Northern Nevada.

NV Energy has disputed recent reports on this, saying the utility’s agreement with Liberty Utilities was always temporary, and it will continue to provide power to residents in South Lake Tahoe while Liberty works to secure alternate sources of energy.

While residents are not expected to lose service outright, the situation has intensified concerns about whether utilities are increasingly prioritizing large industrial users over residential communities as AI infrastructure expands. In states where utilities largely function as state-sanctioned monopolies, residents often have limited alternatives when major grid decisions are made. Critics warn the conflict may foreshadow a broader national challenge as utilities struggle to accommodate the growing energy demands of artificial intelligence.

The long-term buildout of new energy infrastructure also raises questions about Nevada’s climate goals. Rapid expansion of grid capacity could complicate the state’s efforts to reach its target of 50% renewable electricity by 2030.

But beyond the immediate concerns about grid strain is another unresolved question: who pays for the infrastructure needed to sustain the AI boom? As utilities invest in new transmission lines and power generation to accommodate data centers, some critics worry the costs could eventually be spread across the broader public through higher electric rates and long-term grid expansion costs.
Who Controls the West’s New Boom?

The rapid expansion of data centers across Nevada has generated growing concern over water use, electricity demand, and the long-term pressures placed on communities already navigating drought, housing strain, and infrastructure growth. But the story is not simply one of unchecked extraction.

At the same time, the rapid expansion of data centers may also bring significant economic opportunities to the state. Google says it has invested more than $2.3 billion in Nevada since 2019. State and local officials increasingly view data centers as part of Nevada’s long-term economic future, particularly as industries tied to artificial intelligence continue expanding across the country.

But public skepticism remains high. Recent polling found that roughly seven in 10 Americans oppose the construction of AI data centers in their local communities, reflecting broader unease not only about artificial intelligence itself, but about the scale and speed of the infrastructure being built around it.
That tension is beginning to shape policy in Reno.

On May 14, over 80 residents, including organizers from the Water Over Data Alliance, attended the Reno City Council meeting to raise concerns about the rapid expansion of data centers across the region. After hours of public comment, the council voted to approve a pending moratorium, putting a 30-day pause on new conditional use permits for data centers within city limits. Much of the testimony centered on the need for stronger Tribal involvement in the process. In response, city officials committed to direct engagement with Tribal Nations, recognizing them as sovereign governments with a stake in how land and water are managed.
The Council will vote on a final moratorium June 1.
But even though they supported Thursday’s decision—a Nevada local government’s most significant response yet to the increasingly divisive industry—they say the work is nowhere near done.

“A moratorium is only as good as the regulations that are adopted,” said Olivia Tanager, the director of the Sierra Club Toiyabe Chapter, which has called for Reno to pump the brakes on data center permitting for more than a year.

Across the broader West, the data center boom is increasingly being pulled in different directions by competing interests—developers, scientists, Indigenous communities, utilities, and local governments—all with different stakes in how the region’s resources are used.

But the core debate is often misplaced. The debate is not whether data centers extract water, energy or land, because they certainly do. The more important question is whether the systems that govern those resources are equipped to handle this new scale of demand. And, when they are not, what it would actually take to fix them.

New frameworks and policies may help reduce impacts at the margins, but they don’t resolve the underlying issue of governance capacity: who sets the rules, how those rules are enforced, and whether they still make sense under rapidly changing conditions.

Figuring that out requires a different kind of conversation than the one we are having now, one focused less on broad opposition or unchecked expansion, and more on whether the West’s existing institutions can actually manage what is being built on top of them.
With each new boom in the West, the defining question remains the same: who controls the land, water and power that make it possible?

2026-05-17T07:00:00Z,New NRG Energy CEO leans into growth with ‘bring your own power’ for the AI boom and ‘virtual power plants’
column2: Fortune,"Robert Gaudette took over as the new CEO of power and electricity giant NRG Energy at the end of April ready to ride the AI wave and build the “bespoke desires and needs” of hyperscalers nationwide.

column1: But NRG isn’t only in the business of rapidly building new power plants—primarily gas-fired facilities—to satiate the hunger of data centers. NRG also is leaning into the burgeoning business of turning the United States’ dumb power grid smart with better technology and efficiency.

That’s where demand-response programs and so-called “virtual power plants” come into play, convincing both industrial users and residential customers to turn their thermostats over to AI at times of peak demand—and returning excess renewable energy back to the grid if available—to save energy and keep energy prices lower, essentially acting as a de facto power plant.

NRG (No. 153 on the Fortune 500) represents a tale of two strategies—rapid power growth to satisfy demand and smarter grid efficiency to help solve the rising utility bill woes that are triggering AI backlashes nationwide.

“We’ve barely started the first inning from a VPP-virtual power plant perspective,” Gaudette told Fortune in a sit-down interview. “Where we are today is now we have an affordability issue. Now we have a need. You have the combination of technology, willingness, and the economic desire to find a way to mobilize the power of the consumer to make a difference.”
Scaling up quickly

Early this year, NRG closed the roughly $10 billion acquisition of 18 natural gas-fired power plants from LS Power, nearly doubling NRG’s power generation nationwide. NRG also recently partnered with GE Vernova and Kiewit for 5.4 gigawatts—enough to power 4 million homes—of gas-fired turbines to power data center campuses.

Gaudette is leaning into those two acronyms, VPP and BYOP—bring your own power—paid for by hyperscalers and built by NRG. “NRG is uniquely positioned with two attacks on how we solve the challenges,” he said.
NRG is pushing for AI complexes in Texas, but Gaudette insists there are no limitations. New AI deals are expected later this year.

“They can go anywhere in the country. We haven’t been specific about where we would think the first project would be,” Gaudette said. “We have talked to our investors about the benefits of building down here [in Texas]. It’s one market; it’s one government; it’s one permitting regime. But we can take them wherever our customer wants and where we think it makes the most sense.
“From a speed perspective and getting things done—and getting the data center built—Texas has a lot of advantages,” he added.
Houston-based NRG has its power plants in Texas, the Northeast, Midwest, and a handful of facilities in California.

The moves to scale up with LS power plants and partner with GE made NRG a Wall Street darling as the power sector boomed. But the deal also—more quietly—came with LS’ CPower demand-response business for commercial and industrial (C&I) customers. The CPower tagline is: “Your energy assets have value. We pay you to unlock it.”

Likewise, NRG recently introduced a residential VPP program with its Vivint smart home and Reliant retail electricity businesses. NRG gives away smart doorbells and thermostats for contracted participants.

“We’ve never harnessed the power of the load. We have never gone out of our way to help those people who are using the electricity to use it smarter, to use less of it, and to be more thoughtful about how they do it,” Gaudette said. “It’s hard, and there hasn’t been technology to do it. We’re in a different place now.”
The C&I customers were already moving in this direction.

“We have entire teams that work directly with big customers like that, and we’ve been doing that for a decade,” Gaudette said. “It’s not just around traditional-demand response, but also, ‘Just maybe you should schedule your maintenance outage for next weekend, because it looks like it’s going be very hot and prices are going to be very high.’
“What technology has done is now you can take that same thought process and apply it across a million homes. That’s the big change.”
Rapid changes

The acquisition of Vivint was originally considered a boondoggle by investors and contributed to a previous CEO’s ouster over two years ago. But now it’s considered a key part of the growth story. NRG chairman Larry Coben took over as CEO in late 2023, stabilized the company, and led the LS deal.
But Coben’s leadership was always temporary, handing over the reins to Gaudette, a corporate president who’s been with NRG and predecessor companies for 25 years.

A Houston native and Army veteran—a platoon leader removing mines in Bosnia—Gaudette started as an energy trader with Mirant, which was acquired by NRG in 2012—a few years after it tried and failed to buy NRG.

“The military is its own graduate school—the people, leadership, and stress,” he said with a laugh. “It probably helped me a lot when I was on the trading floor in all of the commodity cycles that we’ve been over through the last 20 years.”
And now the power business is looking strong. NRG’s stock is up nearly 60% in 24 months. However, that overall rise includes a nearly 20% in 2026 down to a market cap of about $27 billion.
NRG’s first-quarter earnings fell short of expectations due to high supply costs during Winter Storm Fern and, alternatively, mild winter weather in Texas.
But those are seasonal factors. What Wall Street wants is for NRG to start announcing some big AI deals and build those 5.4 gigawatts of power—and more.

After all, NRG aimed to complete 20 megawatts of VPP power last year. Instead, it achieved 200 megawatts. NRG recently announced plans to add more than 1 gigawatt of battery storage power to its systems. The constraints that shape the AI-driven land rush are not mysteries. They are specific, identifiable, and for the most part well understood by the people who build and operate the grid. The question is whether they can be solved on the timeline the market demands.

Before a new power plant or energy storage facility can connect to the grid, it must go through a series of impact studies and receive approval from a regional transmission operator or utility. As of the end of 2025, over 2,060 gigawatts of generation and storage capacity were seeking connection to the U.S. grid, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's ""Queued Up"" report. For context, that figure is about double the capacity of the entire existing U.S. power plant fleet.

The queue is large, but most projects in it will never be built. Only 13% of the capacity that submitted interconnection requests from 2000 to 2019 had reached commercial operations by the end of 2024; 77% had been withdrawn. The projects that do get built take far longer than they once did. The time projects spend in queues before reaching commercial operation has doubled, from less than two years for projects built in 2000-2007 to over four years for those built in 2018-2024.

In PJM Interconnection, the regional transmission organization serving 13 states and the District of Columbia, the timeline is even worse. The average time from interconnection application to commercial operation has risen from less than two years in 2008 to over eight years in 2025, according to an analysis by RMI, the clean energy research organization.

PJM's 2025 long-term load forecast projects peak load growth of 32 gigawatts from 2024 to 2030, with about 30 gigawatts coming from data centers. That forecast has made PJM ground zero for the collision between demand velocity and grid constraints. In 2025, FERC implemented its Order No. 2023 generator interconnection reforms and accepted pathways to fast-track more than 50 gigawatts of new generation. Even after projects clear the interconnection queue, they face a physical constraint: the equipment needed to build the grid is not available in sufficient quantities.

This surging transformer demand has created a significant supply deficit, with domestic manufacturing capacity unable to keep pace,"" said Ben Boucher, senior analyst at Wood Mackenzie. By comparison, nearly 4,000 miles were built in 2013 alone.

Building time adds to that. FERC's Order No. 1920, adopted in May 2024, reformed regional transmission planning and cost allocation, but compliance deadlines for transmission providers have been extended, and new construction remains years away.

""We're seeing a serious mismatch between where we are and where we need to be.""

The mismatch is not one problem but several, running in parallel: Queues that take years to clear. Equipment that takes years to procure. Transmission lines that take a decade to build. And demand that can materialize in a fraction of that time.

EPRI now projects U.S. data centers could consume 9% to 17% of national electricity by 2030. The range is wide, reflecting genuine uncertainty about AI adoption rates, efficiency gains, and the number of planned facilities that will actually be built. That principle now competes with the physical reality that building the grid to serve those consumers takes time, and the market may not be willing to wait.",Quartz,energy
